questions.stem: Which Veda is called the 'book of melodies' and consists largely of hymns drawn from the Rig Veda set to musical notation?

options.text: Atharva Veda
Sama Veda
Yajur Veda
Brahmana Veda

questions.explanation: The Sama Veda is called the 'book of melodies' or 'Veda of chants'. About 75 of its 1,875 verses are original; the rest are taken from the Rig Veda and set to musical notes (sāman) for chanting during soma sacrifices. The Atharva Veda contains charms and spells; Yajur Veda contains sacrificial formulas.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The tribal assembly in the Vedic period described as the 'general popular assembly of all the people' was called:

options.text: Sabha
Vidatha
Samiti
Parishad

questions.explanation: The Samiti was the general assembly of the entire tribal community and was more democratic. The Sabha was a smaller, more select council of elders and noble warriors. Vidatha was the oldest assembly mentioned in the Rig Veda with military, religious and social functions. Parishad was an advisory body.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The most sacred and frequently mentioned river in the Rig Veda is:

options.text: Saraswati
Ganga
Yamuna
Sindhu (Indus)

questions.explanation: The Saraswati is described as the greatest river (naditame, best of mothers) and occurs hundreds of times in the Rig Veda. The Ganga appears only once in the Rig Veda (in the Nadistuti hymn, 10.75). The Sindhu is important but Saraswati holds the most sacred status. By the Later Vedic period the Saraswati had begun to dry up and the Ganga gained prominence.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Vedic term 'Gramini' referred to:

options.text: The royal priest of the king
The commander of the army
The head of the treasury
The village headman

questions.explanation: Gramini was the village headman responsible for administering the Grama (village), the smallest unit of Vedic administration. The Purohita was the royal priest; Senani was the army commander; Gramani later came to mean leader of a village group. The administrative hierarchy was: Rashtra (kingdom) → Jana (tribe) → Vish (clan) → Grama (village).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which type of pottery is archaeologically associated with the Later Vedic (Aryans') eastward expansion into the Gangetic plain?

options.text: Painted Grey Ware (PGW)
Black and Red Ware (BRW)
Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW)
Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP)

questions.explanation: Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture (c. 1200–600 BCE) is archaeologically associated with the Later Vedic Aryans. PGW sites are found mainly in the Punjab, Haryana, and upper Gangetic plains at places like Hastinapura and Ahichhatra. NBPW is associated with the later Mahajanapada period; OCP with pre-Vedic/early Rig Vedic times; BRW with pre-Mauryan southern India.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Upanishads are collectively known by which philosophical term that means 'end of the Vedas'?

options.text: Brahmanas
Aranyakas
Vedanta
Samhitas

questions.explanation: The Upanishads are called Vedanta, meaning 'end (anta) of the Vedas', both literally (as the final texts in the Vedic corpus) and philosophically (as the culmination and essence of Vedic thought). They expound the concepts of Brahman (universal consciousness) and Atman (individual soul). There are traditionally 108 Upanishads; 13 are considered Mukhya (principal).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Ashvamedha was a grand Vedic ritual. Which of the following best describes it?

options.text: A harvest festival to propitiate rain gods
A royal horse sacrifice performed to assert sovereignty over neighboring kingdoms
A coronation ceremony involving oath-taking before the tribal assembly
A new year ritual to renew the king's mandate

questions.explanation: The Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) was the highest royal sacrifice described in the Yajur Veda. A consecrated horse was set free to roam for one year; any king who challenged it had to fight. After the year, the horse was sacrificed and the king's sovereignty over all conquered territories was ritually established. It symbolised the king's power over the four directions.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: In the Rig Vedic social order, the fourfold varna division (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) was primarily determined by:

options.text: Occupation — a person's varna reflected their chosen profession
Birth — one was born into a varna and could not change it
Ritual purity levels as assessed by the Purohita
Wealth — the wealthiest families became Brahmins

questions.explanation: In the early Rig Vedic period, varna was primarily occupational and relatively flexible. The Purusha Sukta (Rig Veda 10.90) describes the four varnas as emerging from different parts of the cosmic being. Birth-based rigidity intensified only in the Later Vedic period. Historians distinguish the fluid Rig Vedic jati concept from the later birth-determined caste hierarchy.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Brahmanas are a category of Vedic texts. They primarily contain:

options.text: Philosophical discourses on the nature of Brahman and Atman
Popular charms, spells and folk beliefs
Detailed prose explanations of Vedic rituals and sacrificial procedures
Grammar rules and linguistic analysis of Sanskrit

questions.explanation: Brahmanas are prose texts appended to each Veda that explain the meaning and procedures of Vedic rituals. Examples include Shatapatha Brahmana (associated with Yajur Veda), Aitareya Brahmana (Rig Veda), and Chandogya Brahmana (Sama Veda). Philosophical content is in the Upanishads; charms are in the Atharva Veda; forest meditations are in the Aranyakas.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which Veda exists in two major recensions — the Krishna (Black) and Shukla (White) — reflecting two different schools of transmission?

options.text: Rig Veda
Sama Veda
Atharva Veda
Yajur Veda

questions.explanation: The Yajur Veda (Veda of sacrificial formulas) is divided into Krishna Yajur Veda (Black — where prose commentary is mixed with mantras; e.g., Taittiriya Samhita) and Shukla Yajur Veda (White — mantras separate from commentary; e.g., Vajasaneyi Samhita). The Rig Veda has only one main recension; the Sama and Atharva Vedas do not have Black/White divisions.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Rajasuya sacrifice in the Later Vedic period was performed specifically to:

options.text: Ceremonially consecrate a king at the beginning of his reign
Assert victory after a successful military campaign
Propitiate rain gods before the ploughing season
Mark the death anniversary of a previous king

questions.explanation: The Rajasuya was the royal consecration ceremony performed at the beginning of a king's reign (or to re-establish sovereignty). It lasted for over a year and involved elaborate rituals including gambling games, a symbolic cattle raid, and anointing. Yudhishthira's Rajasuya in the Mahabharata is a famous literary reference. The Ashvamedha was for asserting territorial sovereignty; Vajapeya was a rejuvenation sacrifice.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 'Gotra' system, which traced common patrilineal descent from a Vedic sage and prohibited marriage within the same gotra, became prominent during:

options.text: The Rig Vedic period (c. 1500–1000 BCE)
The Later Vedic period (c. 1000–600 BCE)
The Mauryan period (321–185 BCE)
The Gupta period (320–550 CE)

questions.explanation: The Gotra system (patrilineal lineage groups traced to a founding Vedic rishi) developed and became socially significant during the Later Vedic period as society became more settled and caste boundaries hardened. The Rig Vedic tribal society was more fluid. The system was later codified in the Dharmashastra texts but its social practice solidified in Later Vedic times.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: 'Aranyakas' in the Vedic literature are best described as:

options.text: Hymns composed to praise Vedic nature deities
Magical spells and charms for everyday life
Grammatical treatises on Classical Sanskrit
Forest texts that bridge ritual (Brahmanas) and philosophical speculation (Upanishads), composed by forest hermits

questions.explanation: Aranyakas ('forest books') were composed by forest-dwelling hermits (aranyavasis). They occupy an intermediate position between the Brahmanas (focused on ritual detail) and the Upanishads (focused on metaphysics). The Aranyakas begin to allegorize and internalize rituals — for example, the Aitareya Aranyaka of the Rig Veda. The name reflects that they were studied in the forest, away from society.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Rig Vedic 'family books' (Mandalas II–VII) are considered the oldest core of the text because:

options.text: They mention iron tools, which date them to 1500 BCE
They are written in prose while later Mandalas use verse
They preserve the hymns of specific priestly families, handed down continuously within those lineages for generations, with internal consistency in style and deity preference
They contain hymns added after the philosophical Mandalas I and X

questions.explanation: Mandalas II–VII are called family books because each is associated with a specific priestly clan: Gritsamada (II), Vishvamitra (III), Vamadeva (IV), Atri (V), Bharadvaja (VI), Vasishtha (VII). Their internal stylistic consistency and family authorship mark them as the oldest. Mandalas I, VIII, IX, X are later compilations. Iron ('Krishna ayas') appears in the Later Vedic texts, not the Rig Veda core.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which Vedic ceremony marked the formal initiation of a student (usually a boy) into the Guru-shishya relationship, symbolised by wearing the sacred thread?

options.text: Vivaha (marriage ceremony)
Namakarana (naming ceremony)
Annaprashana (first solid food feeding)
Upanayana (sacred thread ceremony)

questions.explanation: Upanayana (from Sanskrit upa = near, nayana = lead) was the rite of passage that led a student to the guru's house for education. It involved the student receiving the yagnopavita (sacred thread) as a symbol of entering the brahmacharya (student) ashrama. This was a key Later Vedic institution that reinforced varna distinctions (it was available only to the first three varnas — dvijas or 'twice-born').
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Vajapeya sacrifice, performed in the Later Vedic period to rejuvenate royal power, notably involved:

options.text: A chariot race in which the king's chariot was required to win ritually
Offering of gold ingots to the presiding deity
A mass sacrifice of one hundred cattle
Ritual ploughing of a sacred field by the king

questions.explanation: Vajapeya ('drink of strength/vigour') was a rejuvenation and royal-prestige sacrifice that included a symbolic chariot race with 17 chariots, in which the king's chariot was ritually arranged to win. It was simpler than the Rajasuya and could be performed by a king seeking to reassert or strengthen his position. The name refers to a ritual soma drink that accompanied the ceremony.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Comparing the position of women in the Rig Vedic and Later Vedic periods, historians generally conclude that:

options.text: Women's status improved significantly in the Later Vedic period due to expanded ritual roles
Women's status remained unchanged throughout both periods
Women's status declined in the Later Vedic period as society became more settled and patriarchal, with restrictions on education and remarriage increasing
Women gained political power in the Later Vedic period through the Samiti assembly

questions.explanation: In the Rig Vedic period, women (brahmavadinis like Gargi, Maitreyi, Lopamudra) could study the Vedas, participate in tribal assemblies (sabha and samiti), and widow remarriage (niyoga) was accepted. In the Later Vedic period, with settled agriculture, rigid varna stratification, and elaborate ritual economy, women's access to education narrowed, child marriage increased, and widow remarriage became restricted.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 'Purohita' in the Vedic political system was:

options.text: The military commander responsible for war strategy
The royal priest and the king's most important political advisor, whose approval was essential for major decisions
The village headman who collected taxes for the king
The superintendent of the royal treasury

questions.explanation: The Purohita ('one placed before') was the royal chaplain who performed all major rituals for the king and was his most trusted counsellor. The Aitareya Brahmana states the king 'fails and falls' without a purohita. Famous purohitas include Vasishtha (purohita to the Ikshvakus) and Vishvamitra. The Senani was the military chief; the Gramini was the village head.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Atharva Veda is distinct from the three 'higher' Vedas primarily because it:

options.text: Contains the oldest hymns of the entire Vedic corpus
Is composed entirely in prose, unlike the other three which use verse
Contains charms, spells, healing incantations, and reflects popular religion outside the high sacrificial tradition
Is structured as dialogues between a teacher and student about the nature of reality

questions.explanation: The Atharva Veda (associated with the Atharvans and Angirases) is sometimes called the 'Veda of magic'. It contains incantations for healing diseases, exorcising demons, winning love, ensuring prosperity, and harming enemies. It reflects the folk religion and everyday concerns of ordinary people alongside the aristocratic soma-sacrifice tradition. For this reason, it was initially not included in the Vedic canon by orthodox tradition.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The concept of 'Brahman' as the ultimate, impersonal, universal reality underlying all existence was primarily elaborated in the:

options.text: Rig Vedic Samhitas (hymn collections)
Yajur Vedic Brahmanas (ritual manuals)
Aranyakas (forest texts)
Upanishads (philosophical treatises)

questions.explanation: The Upanishads (c. 800–200 BCE) are the primary philosophical texts discussing Brahman (the ultimate universal reality) and Atman (the individual self), and the teaching that Atman = Brahman (Tat Tvam Asi — 'That Thou Art'). This philosophy is called Advaita (non-dualism). The Samhitas are hymns; the Brahmanas are ritual guides; the Aranyakas are transitional texts between ritual and philosophy.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Consider the two Vedic assemblies: Sabha and Samiti. Which of the following correctly distinguishes their character?

options.text: Sabha was the larger general assembly of all adult males; Samiti was the restricted inner council of nobles and elders
Sabha was the smaller, more aristocratic council of elders and nobles; Samiti was the larger, more democratic general assembly of the people
Sabha and Samiti were two names for the same assembly and performed identical functions
Sabha was a judicial body that tried crimes; Samiti was exclusively a legislative body that passed laws

questions.explanation: Most historians (including A.L. Basham) distinguish: Sabha = a select council of elders, nobles, and the learned (smaller, aristocratic), and Samiti = the larger general popular assembly. Both had significant powers — the Sabha could overrule the king on important matters and the Samiti elected the king. Their powers gradually weakened in the Later Vedic period as kingship became hereditary and more powerful.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: A student observes that the Ganga is mentioned only once in the Rig Veda yet becomes the most sacred river in Later Vedic and post-Vedic literature. The most historically defensible explanation is:

options.text: Early Aryan settlements were concentrated in the Sapta Sindhu (seven-rivers) region of Punjab; the Ganga gained sacred prominence as Aryan culture migrated eastward into the Gangetic plain during the Later Vedic period
The Ganga was considered ritually impure in the Rig Vedic period and was purified through a series of later ceremonies
Later Vedic priests deliberately edited the Rig Veda to remove Ganga references that threatened Saraswati's supremacy
The Ganga was confused with the Saraswati in early texts because both flowed through the same region

questions.explanation: Archaeological and textual evidence shows that early Vedic culture was centred in Punjab and the Saraswati-Sindhu basin ('Sapta Sindhu' = land of seven rivers). The Rig Vedic hymns reflect this geography. As Aryan settlements expanded eastward during the Later Vedic period (Painted Grey Ware zone: western Gangetic plain), the Ganga became central to religious life, finding prominence in texts like the Shatapatha Brahmana and eventually in the Puranas.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Later Vedic texts begin to use 'ayas' (metal) with the qualifier 'shyama' or 'Krishna' (dark/black), believed by historians to refer to iron. The archaeological basis for associating Later Vedic Aryans with iron technology rests primarily on:

options.text: Iron arrowheads found exclusively in Rig Vedic burial mounds at Mohenjo-daro
Meluhha inscriptions describing an iron trade route between Punjab and West Asia
Iron artifacts (including iron slag, tongs, and tools) found co-occurring with Painted Grey Ware at sites like Hastinapura, Atranjikhera, and Ahichhatra
Ashokan pillar inscriptions that credit Vedic artisans with inventing iron smelting

questions.explanation: Excavations at PGW (Painted Grey Ware) sites — Hastinapura (B.B. Lal, 1950s), Atranjikhera, and Ahichhatra in the upper Gangetic valley — have yielded iron objects (nails, slag, arrow-heads) alongside PGW pottery. Since PGW culture is associated with Later Vedic Aryans, this forms the archaeo-textual link. India entered the Iron Age around 1000–800 BCE corresponding to the Later Vedic period.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Among the principal (Mukhya) Upanishads, the oldest prose Upanishad — and one of the longest — which elaborates the Brahman-Atman identity through dialogue between Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi, is:

options.text: Katha Upanishad
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
Chandogya Upanishad
Mandukya Upanishad

questions.explanation: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (associated with the Shatapatha Brahmana of the Shukla Yajur Veda) is generally considered the oldest and largest principal Upanishad. Its famous dialogues include Yajnavalkya's discussion with his wife Maitreyi about the immortal self (Atman) and the Neti Neti ('not this, not this') approach to Brahman. The Chandogya (Sama Veda) is nearly as old and contains 'Tat Tvam Asi'.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Ashvamedha sacrifice is INCORRECT?

options.text: A consecrated horse was released to roam freely for one year, accompanied by royal warriors
Any king who stopped or captured the horse was required to fight the accompanying army or submit to the performer's sovereignty
It was considered the most powerful of all Vedic sacrifices and could be performed only by a very powerful king
The Ashvamedha is primarily described in the Sama Veda and is not mentioned in the Yajur Veda

questions.explanation: Options A, B, and C are correct descriptions of the Ashvamedha. Option D is INCORRECT: the Ashvamedha is detailed in the Yajur Veda (particularly the Vajasaneyi Samhita and Shatapatha Brahmana) and in the Atharva Veda, not primarily in the Sama Veda. The Sama Veda is the Veda of melodies and is primarily concerned with musical chanting for soma rituals, not horse sacrifice procedures.
questions.subject: History
